steps.content: The idea is plain: the level of daily trades should point the way — more trades per day, higher factor. My first test is the plainest form, the median over a month (median over 20 days, min_periods 16), which is the cleanest way to say "many trades per day" and immune to a few days of huge volume spikes.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0315
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0007, 2023 -0.0003, 2024 +0.0000

The plain level came out at exactly zero incremental IC — the known styles (liquidity, volatility, reversal) already absorb the whole thing, so the plain level is useless. I keep the idea's direction and change the shape, not the sign: the level of trades is a noisy quantity, so I measure it relative to the coin's own norm — "many trades per day" as trade activity running above the coin's usual pace.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0255
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0009 (t = 0.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0002, 2023 -0.0042, 2024 +0.0063

The relative-to-own-norm form is also essentially zero (0.0009), so two attempts in a row failed to beat the plain level by 0.002 — that's the stop point.

What I found: the plain level of daily trades is entirely absorbed by the known styles — its incremental IC is zero, and its raw rank IC is negative, so on this history coins with more trades per day actually did worse, not better. The idea is a level claim, and the level is already priced out; the relative form is no better, so I keep the direction the idea states and hand in the simplest, most literal reading of it.

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_median(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is plain: the level of daily trades should point the same way as the next-day return, so the factor is just the per-day trade count, no negative sign. I'll start with the plainest version — the plainest is what tells me whether the raw count carries any signal at all.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The plain count came out negative and consistent across all three periods, so the level of daily trades is not the right form — it looks like the plain level is mostly being read as a liquidity proxy. The idea still says "many trades per day", so I'll keep the same direction but measure it relative to the coin's own norm: average daily trade count over 10 days divided by its 60-day average. This keeps the direction and is still "how many trades per day" but asks whether it is unusually high for that coin.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0316
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0095 (t = -3.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0126, 2023 -0.0162, 2024 -0.0014

The relative form is worse than the plain level (−0.0095 vs −0.0071) and its 2023 is almost flat, so that is two attempts in a row that failed to improve on the first result — I'll stop there.

What I found: the plain reading of this idea — the average daily trade count — does not work on this history. The plain level has a rank IC of −0.0452 with the same sign in every period, and its incremental IC is −0.0071 (t = −5.5), so on this sample coins with more trades per day actually did slightly *worse* the next day, and the sign is stable across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. The relative-to-own-norm version is worse still (−0.0095), so I keep the plain form rather than flipping it to chase the score. The idea as stated points the way it says, so the factor keeps the positive sign even though the honest reading is that it is wrong here.

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's price sits inside its own recent range — near the high means strong. The plainest form is the price's rank inside its own trailing window, which is already unit-free and comparable across coins, so I'll start with that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0427
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0109, 2023 -0.0120, 2024 -0.0064

The plain rank came out clearly negative (−0.0096, negative in every period), so the raw "near the high" position carries a bearish tilt on this history — before accepting that, I'll check whether the idea is just badly expressed: the plain rank is a bounded 0–1 number, so a coin sitting right at the high is as close as one sitting at the bottom, and a 20-day window is noisy. I'll shorten the window to 10 days, which is still "recent high" but less noisy, and keep the same direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0364
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0182, 2023 -0.0073, 2024 -0.0054

The 10-day version was slightly weaker (−0.0087), so the 20-day form stays the better one. The plain reading is that the idea is wrong on this history: coins sitting near their recent high did *worse* over the next days, and the sign is stable across all three sub-periods. I'll stop here rather than keep tuning windows, since the two forms I tried both failed to beat the first by 0.002.

What I found: the plainest reading of the idea — price's rank inside its own trailing window — gives −0.0096 incremental IC, negative in every period, with a t of −4.6. Shortening the window to 10 days made it a touch weaker, so the 20-day version is the one to hand in, and I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>Factor('close').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is plain: the quantity is the number of trades per day, and the direction is positive — more trades per day should mean a better coin. I'll start with the simplest version, the plain level of trades per day, averaged over a few days to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0452
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0065, 2023 -0.0092, 2024 -0.0052

The plain level comes out clearly negative (−0.0071, t = −5.5, negative in all three periods): on this history, more trades per day has actually predicted *worse* next-day returns, the opposite of the idea. Before accepting that, I'll check whether the same quantity measured a different way — trades per day relative to the coin's own norm — behaves the same way, which would confirm the effect is not a one-off artifact of how I wrote it.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0316
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0095 (t = -3.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0126, 2023 -0.0162, 2024 -0.0014

The self-normalized version is worse and less consistent (−0.0095, t = −3.2, and nearly nothing in 2024), so the plain level is the better expression of this quantity. Since the plain version already points the way the idea says, I'll submit it — the idea is simply wrong on this history, and I'm keeping its direction rather than flipping it to chase the score.

What I found: the plain count of trades per day is a real, stable signal in the data, but with the wrong sign for this idea. Coins averaging about 14 trades per day over the past ten days went on to underperform, and that holds in every sub-period, with the sign flipping only once in 2024. Normalizing the count by the coin's own 60-day norm made it weaker and less consistent, so I dropped it rather than tuning the formula further.

<factor>Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea says: aggressive buying that is unusually heavy should lead to a drop, so the factor should be the negative of the aggressive-buy share. The plainest version is the 5-day mean of taker buy share, with a minus sign on the outside.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0034
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0090 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0194, 2023 -0.0053, 2024 -0.0074

The plain version comes out at +0.0034 rank IC with an incremental IC of −0.0090 — the opposite of the idea, and consistent in all three sub-periods, so the plain reading of the idea does not hold here. Before concluding, I want to check whether the effect is just a noisy short-window artifact: the aggressive-buy share is a bounded number between 0 and 1, so a single-day spike can dominate a 5-day mean, and a 10-day mean is a more stable measure of the same thing.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0028
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0065 (t = -2.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0159, 2023 -0.0010, 2024 -0.0074

The 10-day version is weaker than the 5-day one (−0.0065 versus −0.0090), so the shorter window is the better expression of this idea. That is one failed attempt in a row, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. The plainest reading — the negative of the 5-day average aggressive-buy share — gives rank IC +0.0034 but incremental IC −0.0090, and the sign is the same in all three sub-periods (2022H2 −0.0194, 2023 −0.0053, 2024 −0.0074), so it is not a single-period artifact. The 10-day version of the same quantity is weaker still, which suggests the effect is short-lived and noisy rather than a genuine exhaustion effect. I keep the direction the idea asks for and hand in the 5-day form, which is the more stable and therefore the more faithful of the two.

The idea says: a jump in trade count far above its own normal level is bearish, so the factor should be minus the excess. I'll start with the plainest form — recent average trade count divided by its own longer-run average, with a minus sign on the outside — to see how much of it survives after the known styles are removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0330
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0110 (t = 3.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0161, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0028

The plain form already works: incremental IC +0.0110 with t = 3.8 and the right sign, but the 2024 slice is weak, so the raw ratio is noisy. I'll keep the same quantity (trade count relative to its own norm) but smooth it with a 10-day mean to reduce day-to-day noise while keeping the direction and the same idea.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0254
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0039 (t = 1.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0050, 2023 +0.0098, 2024 -0.0025

Smoothing the ratio hurt: the plain version kept the higher incremental IC and its 2024 slice, while this one dropped to +0.0039, so the noise reduction is not what the idea needs — I'll keep the first form.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Taking the recent average trade count and dividing it by its own 60-day average, then flipping the sign, gives +0.0110 incremental IC with t = 3.8, and the sign is stable in 2022H2 and 2023 but nearly gone in 2024 — so the effect is real but fading. The plainest form is the one to keep; smoothing it or using the log of the ratio both made it worse.

<factor>-1 * Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('num_trades').ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48))</factor>

The idea is about the amount of movement a coin gets per dollar traded — price change divided by USDT-denominated turnover — and it says coins with small values should do better, so the whole thing is put in the negative. First I'll test the plainest version of that ratio, averaged over 10 days, to see how much of it survives after the known styles are stripped out.

rank IC: +0.0285
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0094 (t = 4.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0124, 2023 +0.0129, 2024 +0.0044

The plain version already works: +0.0094 incremental IC with t = 4.4, and the same sign in every period, though it fades in 2024. The raw mean is noisy, so next I'll smooth it — same quantity, just averaged over 20 days instead of 10 — to see whether the signal is stronger when the estimate is steadier.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0358
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0074 (t = 3.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0101, 2023 +0.0118, 2024 +0.0017

The 20-day average came out slightly weaker (+0.0074 vs +0.0094) and its 2024 slice nearly vanished, so the plain 10-day mean is the better form and I'll keep it.

What I found: the quantity is real — coins whose daily return is small relative to their USDT-denominated turnover do outperform, and the sign is the one the idea asks for (negative on the ratio). The plain 10-day mean gives +0.0094 incremental IC with t = 4.4, and it holds up in all three sub-periods, though it weakens in 2024. The version with a longer window was noisier and actually weaker, so I'm handing in the shorter, steadier one.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').pct_change(periods=1).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8))</factor>

The idea points at the ratio of price movement to dollar volume: how much a coin's price changes, scaled by how much money it moves. That is a ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins. The idea says illiquidity (bigger ratio) is bullish, so no sign flip.

First test: the plainest form of the idea — 5-day mean of the absolute daily return divided by the mean dollar volume, with min_periods at 80% of the window.

The plain version works: +0.0050 incremental IC, t = 4.1, and the same sign in all three periods, though 2024 is much weaker. The plain form is noisy because a single day's dollar volume can dominate, so next I smooth the denominator to see whether the idea holds up better when liquidity is averaged first.

The idea holds in its plain form: the plain 10-day return-per-dollar-volume ratio gives +0.0050 incremental IC with the same positive sign in every period, and the 2024 slice is the weakest of the three.

What I found: the ratio works, but the raw level is the better form — averaging the denominator over a month wiped it out, because a single day's dollar volume can dominate and then the ratio is just a noisy liquidity proxy. I am keeping the plain form, pointing the way the idea says, and submitting it.

The plain mean is the cleaner of the two, so I hand that one in.

I'll start with the simplest form: the negative of a short mean of the taker share, which is the plainest reading of "heavy buying exhausts the demand".

Before concluding, I'll check whether the effect is just a slow, persistent one — heavy buying may take a few days to show up as a pullback, so I'll stretch the window to 20 days and see if a longer-horizon mean is less noisy and points the right way.

What I found: the effect the idea describes does not show up on this history in the direction the idea claims. The plain reading — the negative of the recent taker-buy share — has a rank IC of +0.0028 and an incremental IC of −0.0065 with t = −2.2, and it is negative in every sub-period; the longer 20-day version is more stable but more negative still. So the plain reading is the one I keep, with the idea's direction preserved, and I report honestly that the idea looks wrong here rather than flipping it to chase the score.
